section_1.title: Prerequisite Review: Conditional Probability
section_1.content: Briefly recap the definition of conditional probability: P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B). Use a visual Venn diagram to show the 'reduction of sample space' when event B is known to have occurred.
section_1.example: A bowl contains 10 fruits: 6 apples (4 red, 2 green) and 4 oranges. Visual highlight: If we know the fruit is an apple, the sample space shrinks from 10 to 6.

section_2.title: The Concept of Independence
section_2.content: Define statistical independence: Events A and B are independent if P(A|B) = P(A). Explain that knowing B gives no information about A. Represent this visually as two separate, non-overlapping circles in a probability space.
section_2.example: Flipping a coin (Event A: Heads) and rolling a die (Event B: Rolling a 6). The outcome of the coin flip does not shift the probability of the die roll.

section_3.title: Introducing Bayes' Theorem
section_3.content: Introduce Bayes' Theorem as a method for 'reversing' conditional probability. Formula: P(A|B) = [P(B|A) * P(A)] / P(B). Use a tree diagram to show how we start from a cause (A) and work backward to evaluate the likelihood of that cause given an effect (B).
section_3.example: A 'Robot Doctor' diagnoses a patient. If the patient has a symptom (B), how do we update the probability of a specific disease (A) based on the test accuracy?

section_4.title: Synthesis: Applying Bayes in Real Scenarios
section_4.content: Connect the concepts: Show how Bayes' Theorem behaves when events are independent versus dependent. Emphasize that Bayes is the engine behind machine learning classifiers like Naive Bayes.
section_4.example: A cat detector algorithm: If the cat is 'Fluffy' (A) and it is 'Daytime' (B), assume independence to simplify the calculation: P(A|B) = P(A). But if B is 'Meowing', independence fails, and we must use the full Bayes' formula to update our belief about which cat is in the room.

section_5.title: Summary & Conclusion
section_5.content: Recap: Independence simplifies probability (multiplication rule), while Bayes' Theorem provides a systematic way to update our beliefs as new evidence arrives. Final visual: A scale balancing prior belief against new evidence.
section_5.example: Final thought: 'Probability is not a fixed number, but a dynamic update.' Use a quick 10-second animation of a 'Belief Bar' moving toward 100% as more evidence is gathered.

outline.example: A cat detector algorithm: If the cat is 'Fluffy' (A) and it is 'Daytime' (B), assume independence to simplify the calculation: P(A|B) = P(A). But if B is 'Meowing', independence fails, and we must use the full Bayes' formula to update our belief about which cat is in the room.
